question: In community nursing, what does a "health need" actually mean?

options.A: The total number of hospital beds available in a district
options.B: The total population size of a specific rural village
options.C: The monthly budget allocated for primary health clinics
options.D: The gap between current health status and a desired healthy state

explanation: Spot on! Think of a health need as the distance between how healthy a community is right now and where they ought to be for good well-being. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why should a community health nurse look at the health needs of a whole group instead of just single patients?

options.A: It helps allocate resources effectively to design meaningful programs
options.B: It guarantees complete eradication of all chronic diseases
options.C: It eliminates the need to ever visit individual households
options.D: It ensures every single citizen receives specialized surgery

explanation: Looking at the big picture helps you focus on what really plagues the population so you can put your limited time and materials to the best possible use! [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which type of health need is decided by healthcare professionals using expert standards?
explanation: You got it! "Normative" comes from norms or standards. These are the needs experts spot based on professional guidelines and research. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h2)

question: A village thinks their stream water is fine, but lab tests show it is full of harmful bacteria. The nurse steps in to treat the water. What kind of need is this?
explanation: Even though the villagers didn't complain, professional testing uncovered the hidden danger. That expert-defined standard makes it a normative need! [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the main reason for doing a community diagnosis?

options.A: To increase hospital admission rates across the state
options.B: To understand root causes of health issues and plan interventions
options.C: To replace individual clinical nursing practice completely
options.D: To punish local leaders for poor environmental sanitation

explanation: Exactly! Just like checking a patient's vitals before giving medicine, a community diagnosis helps you find the root problem so you can plan the right solution. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h3)

question: How is a community diagnosis similar to diagnosing an individual patient in the clinic?

options.A: Both focus exclusively on surgical intervention methods
options.B: Both identify problems to guide the choice of proper treatment or action
options.C: Both require the patient to stay overnight in a hospital bed
options.D: Both rely entirely on laboratory blood work results

explanation: Spot on. Whether it's one patient or a whole village, you have to figure out what is wrong first before you can choose the best way to help. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h3)

question: Before you start collecting data for a community diagnosis, what is usually the very first step?

options.A: Securing administrative clearance and mobilizing stakeholders
options.B: Building a permanent health clinic building
options.C: Writing the final evaluation report for the ministry
options.D: Treating all sick children with antibiotics

explanation: You always want to respect local authority! Getting permission and greeting community leaders comes first before marching in with clipboards. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why do community nurses take their analyzed data back to the community for validation?

options.A: To hide negative health statistics from government officials
options.B: To punish local residents who refused to answer survey questions
options.C: To confirm the accuracy of findings with the community members
options.D: To print extra copies of the survey questionnaire

explanation: Validation is all about checking your homework with the people who live there to make sure your conclusions match their everyday reality. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which of these is an example of secondary data during a community assessment?

options.A: Focus group discussions with village youths
options.B: Interviews conducted with mothers at the market
options.C: Existing clinic registers and census reports
options.D: Direct observation of village water sources

explanation: Correct! Secondary data is information that's already gathered and sitting there waiting for you, like old hospital records and government census books. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the biggest advantage of using qualitative methods like focus group discussions?

options.A: They eliminate the need to ever write a formal report
options.B: They provide deeper insight into cultural beliefs and local attitudes
options.C: They require no active participation from community members
options.D: They give exact numerical percentages of disease outbreaks

explanation: Numbers are great, but talking to people helps you understand the "why" behind their health habits and cultural beliefs! [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h5)

question: A village has issues with both scabies and severe malaria. The nurse prioritizes malaria because it kills many young children. What guiding principle is this?

options.B: Total number of adult males employed

explanation: Spot on! When a condition is life-threatening, its severity and urgency push it straight to the top of your priority list. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is the most important ingredient for a community health program to actually work?

options.C: Complete absence of local traditional healers

explanation: You can have all the funding in the world, but if the local people aren't involved and on board, the program won't last. Community ownership is key! [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h7)

question: Why is it so important to set clear, specific objectives during the planning stage?

options.A: It guides what activities to do and helps measure future success
options.B: It replaces the need to collect baseline data
options.C: It guarantees that no unexpected problems will ever occur
options.D: It ensures that nurses never have to work in rural areas

explanation: Clear objectives act like a map. They show you your daily steps and let you check later whether you actually reached your destination. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h7)

question: How is monitoring different from evaluation in a community health project?

options.A: Monitoring is done only by doctors, while evaluation is done by patients
options.B: Monitoring happens after the project ends, while evaluation happens before
options.C: Monitoring is ongoing review, while evaluation is a periodic impact assessment
options.D: Monitoring focuses only on money, while evaluation focuses only on weather

explanation: Think of monitoring as checking your pulse while running the race, and evaluation as looking at your final race time once you cross the finish line! [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h8)

question: What is the main benefit of sharing your final evaluation results with the community?

options.A: It stops all future health problems from ever returning
options.B: It legally forces every citizen to donate money to the clinic
options.C: It fosters transparency and helps everyone learn lessons for the future
options.D: It proves that the nursing staff made zero errors during the project

explanation: Sharing results builds trust and empowers the community to keep up the good work and learn what to improve next time. [learn more](GNS124_U3_T2#GNS124_U3_T2_h8)
